bib.title: Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits

legacy_report:
**COVERAGE:** All 18 pages read (81,122 chars), including Limitations and Appendices A and B. The references were skimmed. No extraction faults, and no instructions embedded in the text.

**SOURCE:** "Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits", arXiv 2501.01880v1 [cs.CL], dated 27 Dec 2024.
- Authors: Xinze Li, Yubo Ma and Aixin Sun (S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University); Yixin Cao (School of Computer Science, Fudan University). Sun and Cao carry the corresponding-author marks.
- Venue: preprint. I found no venue, conference or journal anywhere in the text. It uses ACL-style formatting, but nothing names a venue.
- Code and data: github.com/lixinze777/LC_VS_RAG.

**Main claim:** Once questions answerable without context are filtered out, long context (LC) generally beats RAG on QA benchmarks, especially for Wikipedia and story sources. Summarization-based retrieval (RAPTOR) comes closest and chunk-based retrieval lags. RAG wins on dialogue and yes/no "Other" questions, and conflicting earlier results are partly explained by context relevance, retriever choice and small samples.

**Headline numbers**
1. **LC vs RAG, strict exact match (EM).** LC answered 56.3% of 13,628 filtered questions correctly and RAG 49.0%. The counts are 7,676 vs 6,683. LC-only wins were 2,287 and RAG-only wins 1,294, so almost 10% of questions only RAG gets right.
   - Setup: RAG used RAPTOR; the same LLM answers both arms, which Table 6 shows is GPT-4o or GPT-4-Turbo. The text never names the model for the main Table 4 run.
   - Loose evaluation (EM or higher F1): LC better on 3,433 questions, RAG better on 1,843.
   - Truncation: for LC, context is truncated from the back if it exceeds the window.
2. **Retriever selection.** Run on a sample set of about 1,563 filtered questions (my inference from 602 = 38.5%): RAPTOR 38.5% correct (602), Window Parsing 35.5%, Tree Index 30.1%, text-embedding-3-small 21.6%, BM25 20.4%, Contriever 20.1%. Swapping GPT-4o for GPT-4-Turbo as generator moved RAPTOR only from 38.5% to 37.7%.
3. **Filtering and expansion.** GPT-4o with strict EM removed questions it answers without context. 12 datasets, 19,188 questions after expansion with distractor passages, 13,628 kept (71%). The text says 13,651 once; Table 3 says 13,628.
   - Keep rates: Coursera 32%, NQ 34%, QuALITY and TOEFL-QA 100%.
4. **By source and question type (EM, only-LC vs only-RAG counts).** Wikipedia 873 vs 348, Story 842 vs 391, Paper/Report 531 vs 507, Dialogue 31 vs 44. "Other" (yes/no) questions favour RAG, 54 LC-only vs 140 RAG-only.

**Quotes**
- p.1, abstract: "We show that LC generally outperforms RAG in question-answering benchmarks, especially for Wikipedia-based questions. Summarization-based retrieval performs comparably to LC, while chunk-based retrieval lags behind."
- p.6, §5.2: "Overall, LC correctly answers 56.3% of the questions, while RAG provides correct answers to 49.0%."
- p.6: "almost 10% can be only answered correctly by RAG... retrievers cannot be simply replaced by long-context LLM in searching."

The abstract's "comparably" for RAPTOR is looser than Table 5 allows. Table 5 is a retriever-vs-retriever comparison on the sample set and has no LC column.

**Limits**
- The authors concede three limits: text only, only retrievers and LLMs from the surveyed papers, and newer models or retrievers may change the outcome.
- Only GPT-4o and GPT-4-Turbo are used as generators; "other models... in progress".
- Wikipedia contexts are synthetic, built by adding noise to create long context. The authors say this is partly RAG-like and may bias against RAG, so the Wikipedia LC advantage is confounded.
- Chunk size and top-k for RAG are not specified in what I read, and there is no cost or latency comparison.
- The authors say they cannot promise RAPTOR beats all retrieval strategies. No relevance feedback or query expansion was tried.
- Contexts average 0.7K to 67K words, so the paper does not test the 100K to 1M token regime.
- Figures 3 and 4 are word counts of question subsets (not accuracy), and there are no confidence intervals.
- The yes/no explanation (training-data familiarity) is a hypothesis.

**Builds on (as printed)**
- LongBench (Bai et al., 2024a); LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2024b).
- Xu et al. 2024b, Retrieval meets LC LLMs: LC beats 4K-context RAG on multi-hop; best with top-5 to top-10 chunks.
- LongRAG (Jiang et al., 2024b); ChatQA2 (Xu et al., 2024a), where RAG beats LC up to 32K.
- Self-ROUTE (Li et al., 2024), where LC always beats RAG but RAG is cheaper. Per the paper, RAG and LC give the same answers on about 60% of questions there.
- OP-RAG (Yu et al., 2024), "In defense of RAG"; LC LLM meets RAG (Jin et al., 2024); Leng et al. 2024, LC RAG performance.
- Retrievers: RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024), BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009), Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022), Llama-Index (Liu, 2022).
- Datasets include L-Eval (An et al., 2024) and NovelQA (Wang et al., 2024a).

**Figures:** The paper has a Figure 2 evaluation matrix (win/lose categories) and Table 1, a useful summary of the conflicting earlier findings. I did not run the captions script.
